In this chapter and the next, we'll cover the techniques of correlation and regression. Whereas the techniques we've covered so far deal with examining differences between groups, correlation and regression focus on associations between variables. As we'll see, though, this isn't as big a difference as you might expect. Correlation and regression are just another extension of the basic ideas of variability, sampling, and probability that have powered all of our inferential statistics so far.

## From groups to pairs

The key difference between the correlational approach and the designs and statistical tests we've covered so far---the $t$ test and ANOVA approach---is that those other approaches compare groups. This means studies with a grouping variable: a categorical variable that divides the sample up into different conditions, whether by random assignment or not. The statistics then compare those groups looking for differences over and above what we'd expect by chance. Correlational studies measure two quantitative variables per participant and examine the relationship between those variables---their association, rather than their difference.

<!-- PLAN: the big difference, made explicit. Comparison table (Chapters 11–16 vs. this chapter: variables, what each person contributes, picture, question, statistic) and the points from the editorial pass: rows are people and both columns are measurements; it looks like related samples but isn't the same question; X and Y are interchangeable; it's less of a break than it looks. -->

## Picturing a relationship

To give a few quick examples of these kinds of psychological research questions, we may be interested in the correlation between a person's income and their happiness. Do wealthier people tend to say they're happier? We generally visualize correlational data as a scatterplot like this: one variable on the $x$ axis and the other on the $y$ axis. Each dot represents one person's pair of scores.

{{< interactive-figure incomeHappinessScatter makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.2,"n":45,"seed":11},"style":"minimal","axisLabels":true,"xLabel":"Income","yLabel":"Happiness","maxWidth":"22rem"}' fallback="Scatterplot of hypothetical income and happiness scores: a loose cloud of dots drifting slightly upward, suggesting that higher income tends to go with somewhat higher happiness." >}}

Another question might be, does practice make perfect? We could record the amount of time someone spent practicing a task and record their performance of the task and put those pairs of observations on a scatterplot. Or we might suspect that the more absences someone has from a class, the worse their final grade will be for that class. Here, unlike those previous two examples, we'd be expecting that higher scores on one variable would be associated with lower scores on the other. This would be a negative correlation.

{{< interactive-figure absencesGradeScatter makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":-0.35,"n":45,"seed":12},"style":"minimal","axisLabels":true,"xLabel":"Absences","yLabel":"Final grade","maxWidth":"22rem"}' fallback="Scatterplot of hypothetical absences and final grades: a loose cloud of dots sloping downward, with more absences tending to go with lower grades: a negative correlation." >}}

### Characteristics of correlations

We'll be calculating a correlation statistic. But before we learn how it's calculated, it's important to outline its general conceptual structure. The correlation statistic is a single number that quantifies the association between two variables. It has three characteristics: its absolute magnitude, its direction, and its form.

#### Magnitude

The absolute magnitude varies from zero to one. This quantifies the strength of the relationship, or, in other words, the consistency of the association between the variables. The stronger and more consistent their association, the closer the correlation will be to 1. The weaker and less consistent their relationship, the closer the correlation will be to 0. In the four diagrams below, I've traced an ellipse around the scattered dots. Basically, the tighter the ellipse you can draw, the stronger the correlation is. Close to zero, it's basically a circle. At a correlation of one, it becomes a straight line, perfectly joining up all the points.

::: {.sfs-figure-row}
{{< interactive-figure magnitudeScatterR0 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = 0: the ellipse traced around the dots is essentially a circle." >}}

{{< interactive-figure magnitudeScatterR40 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.4,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = .40: the ellipse tilts upward but stays wide." >}}

{{< interactive-figure magnitudeScatterR80 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.8,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = .80: a much tighter upward-sloping ellipse." >}}

{{< interactive-figure magnitudeScatterR100 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":1,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Points with r = 1: the ellipse collapses into a straight line joining every point." >}}
:::

#### Direction

The second characteristic is the direction of the correlation, meaning its sign, positive or negative. A positive correlation is one for which increases in one variable are associated with increases on the other---or, correspondingly, lower scores on one are associated with lower scores on the other. A negative correlation means that higher scores on one variable are associated with lower scores on the other---that they move in opposite directions. Below, I've flipped the diagrams around so that they're now illustrating negative correlations.

::: {.sfs-figure-row}
{{< interactive-figure directionScatterR0 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = 0: a circular cloud with no direction either way." >}}

{{< interactive-figure directionScatterR40 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":-0.4,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = −.40: a wide ellipse sloping downward." >}}

{{< interactive-figure directionScatterR80 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":-0.8,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = −.80: a tight downward-sloping ellipse." >}}

{{< interactive-figure directionScatterR100 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":-1,"n":60,"seed":7},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Points with r = −1: a perfect straight line sloping downward." >}}
:::

#### Form

And finally, there is the form of the association. We will only cover linear correlations. This means that we're imagining that the association forms a straight line. For positive correlations, an increase in $X$ is associated with the same average increase in $Y$ all the way along the line. Or for negative correlations, the same average decrease in $Y$.

But there are other forms that correlations can take---nonlinear forms, where the relationship between $X$ and $Y$ is different for different values of $X$. For one set of points, you can imagine a line that curves, so that as $X$ increases, $Y$ decreases, until a certain point where the curve changes direction, and increases in $X$ become associated with increases in $Y$. Or you can imagine even more complex lines which change directions more than once, attempting to find the best fit for the data. There can be value in these approaches, but for our purposes, we're going to focus on the basic linear form of correlation.

<!-- FIGURE: a form row (linear, curved, U-shaped clouds, each with its r). Needs a nonlinear option in the scatterplot generator, or explicit points. -->

### Estimating correlations

A somewhat useful skill to practice is being able to look at a scatterplot and estimate the strength of the correlation. It's actually easier than you'd think. It takes just a very small amount of practice to get quite good.

Here's a very small dataset with just seven data points. It's representing some hypothetical data from a study looking at how much coffee students drank on the morning of an exam and their test score. It sounds plausible that these two things would be correlated.

| Participant | Coffee (cups) | Test score |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 90 |
| B | 0.5 | 60 |
| C | 0.5 | 85 |
| D | 1 | 65 |
| E | 1.5 | 50 |
| F | 1.5 | 65 |
| G | 2 | 75 |

: Cups of coffee on the morning of an exam and test scores (out of 100) for seven students. {#tbl-coffee-scores}

## Building $r$

So now let's examine the actual correlation statistic that we'll be using. It's called Pearson's $r$ correlation coefficient. It was developed by Karl Pearson. There are other variations of correlation statistics, but Pearson's $r$ is by far the most widely used. It's based on the ideas of variability and covariability.

You're very familiar with variability by now. It's the quantification of how much each variable varies, how widely spread or closely clustered scores are. Covariability is the new idea here. It quantifies how much $X$ and $Y$ vary in tandem. To what extent are changes in $X$ associated with corresponding changes in $Y$? So as $X$ increases, $Y$ increases as well, or as $X$ decreases, $Y$ also tends to decrease. Put another way, if there was no covariability, variation in $Y$ would be completely unrelated to the variation in $X$.

### The equation

Here's the equation:

$$ r = \frac{SP}{\sqrt{SS_X SS_Y}} $$ {#eq-pearson-r}

$SS_X$ and $SS_Y$ should look familiar. $SS$, as usual, refers to the sum of squared deviations. So here we have the separate sums of squares for variable $X$ and variable $Y$ to quantify their separate variability in the denominator. And we have this new quantity, $SP$, which quantifies the covariability of $X$ and $Y$.

I'll explain in a moment exactly what $SP$ is. But first, let me point out that if every change in $X$ had a corresponding change in $Y$, then their covariability in the numerator would be exactly as big as their separate variabilities, combined in the denominator. The correlation would equal one or negative one, meaning every change in $X$ is accompanied by a proportional change in $Y$. In other words, all the variability is covariability. There is no variability that isn't shared. So the more unshared variability there is, the lower the correlation coefficient will be, until when there is no shared variability at all, the numerator of the equation will be zero and we will get a correlation coefficient of zero.

### Sum of squares recap

Before getting to $SP$, let's recap sum of squares. To calculate the sum of squared deviations, we square the deviation scores. And another way of saying that we square something is to say we multiply it by itself. So the definitional formula we learned for sums of squares was $\Sigma(X - M)^2$. And another equivalent way of writing that would be $\Sigma(X - M)(X - M)$. $X$ minus the mean gives us the deviations. We multiply those deviations by themselves. The squaring is just a convenient notation for this, but it means the same thing.

### Sum of products ($SP$)

The reason I point this out is that the numerator does something quite similar, but instead of multiplying deviations by themselves, we multiply them by one another. Our numerator, $SP$, is the sum of products. Products refer to the product of the deviations. We multiply the deviations for variable $X$ by the deviations for variable $Y$ to get their products. Then we sum those products to get the sum of products.

The definitional formula for this is $\Sigma(X - M_X)(Y - M_Y)$. And I hope that by juxtaposing it with the sum of squares formula, you can see the conceptual link. The sum of squares quantifies the variability of an individual variable by multiplying its deviations by themselves. The sum of products quantifies the covariability of two variables by multiplying their deviations by one another.[^sp-computational]

[^sp-computational]: As with the sum of squares back in Chapter 4, there's also a computational formula for the sum of products, and it's similarly related: $SP = \Sigma XY - \frac{(\Sigma X)(\Sigma Y)}{n}$. Again, this is equivalent to the definitional formula. We'll stick with the definitional approach.

Before we calculate anything, let's see what the sum of products looks like.

::::: {#act-sum-of-products .callout-tip .interactive .with-controls}

### Worked example

So let's return to the coffee data from @tbl-coffee-scores. The variable labeled $X$ is the number of cups of coffee these seven people said they drank that morning. The variable labeled $Y$ is their score on a test. We want to know if coffee consumption is related to test performance. So we'll calculate the correlation coefficient. We just need these three quantities: the sum of squares for $X$, the sum of squares for $Y$, and the sum of products.

The first thing we need to do is calculate the mean of each variable, then the deviations for $X$ and $Y$, then square those deviations, and then sum the squared deviations to get the sums of squares. This gets us the values for the denominator of the $r$ equation. The last step is to multiply the deviations for $X$ and $Y$ to get the products. So $-1$ multiplied by $20$ gives $-20$, $-0.5$ multiplied by $-10$ gives positive 5, and so on. We then sum those products to get the sum of products, which here is $-30$.

| $X$ | $X - M_X$ | $(X - M_X)^2$ | $Y$ | $Y - M_Y$ | $(Y - M_Y)^2$ | $(X - M_X)(Y - M_Y)$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | $-1$ | 1 | 90 | 20 | 400 | $-20$ |
| 0.5 | $-0.5$ | 0.25 | 60 | $-10$ | 100 | 5 |
| 0.5 | $-0.5$ | 0.25 | 85 | 15 | 225 | $-7.5$ |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 65 | $-5$ | 25 | 0 |
| 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 50 | $-20$ | 400 | $-10$ |
| 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.25 | 65 | $-5$ | 25 | $-2.5$ |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 75 | 5 | 25 | 5 |
| | | $SS_X = 3$ | | | $SS_Y = 1200$ | $SP = -30$ |

: Deviations, squared deviations, and products for the coffee data. $M_X = 1$; $M_Y = 70$. {#tbl-r-definitional}

$$r = \frac{SP}{\sqrt{SS_X SS_Y}} = \frac{-30}{\sqrt{3 \times 1200}} = \frac{-30}{60} = -.50$$

::: {#quiz-correlation-calculate-r}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-calculate-r.qmd >}}
:::

## A correlation test, step by step

So let's dive into a hypothesis test using Pearson's $r$ correlation coefficient.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

As always, we begin by formally stating our hypotheses. And as with every other hypothesis test we've done, we're going to use samples of scores, but we don't actually care about those samples. We're interested in the population or populations that produce them. So our hypotheses concern the relationship that exists or doesn't exist in the population. The lowercase letter $r$ is the correlation coefficient we calculate for our sample. We use the Greek letter $\rho$ to represent the population parameter, the correlation within the population. The null hypothesis says that there's no relationship in the population, so $\rho$ is zero. We'll use a nondirectional alternative, which says that it isn't:

$$ H_0: \rho = 0 $$

$$ H_1: \rho \ne 0 $$

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

Now, this is going to sound weird, but the test statistic for a correlation is actually a $t$ statistic, not the $r$ correlation coefficient that we just calculated. We'll see how to calculate that $t$ statistic in Step 3. But for now, we just need to know its degrees of freedom so we can determine the critical $t$ values. And for bivariate correlations, degrees of freedom are $n$, the number of pairs of scores, minus two. That's because we're dealing with two variables, each with its own mean, so we lose one degree of freedom for each. But these aren't two independent samples. We're looking at the associations between pairs of scores, so $n$ counts the pairs.

As before, we can check the $t$ table to find the critical values. Since our little example dataset has seven pairs of scores, our degrees of freedom are seven minus two, which is five. We'll use $\alpha = .05$. Looking in the two-tailed .05 column gives critical values of $\pm 2.571$. We reject the null if $t < -2.571$ or $t > 2.571$.

::: {#tbl-correlation-critical}
{{< interactive-figure correlationCriticalTable makeTTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the coffee test","df":{"from":1,"to":7},"alphas":[0.1,0.05,0.025,0.01,0.005],"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","confidence":false,"interactive":false,"selected":{"df":5,"tail":"two","alpha":0.05}}' fallback="t table excerpt for 1 through 7 degrees of freedom, highlighting the two-tailed .05 critical value of 2.571 at df = 5." >}}

An excerpt of the $t$ table, with the $df = 5$ row highlighted. The two-tailed $.05$ heading puts $.025$ in each tail.
:::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

So next, we need the correlation coefficient, Pearson's $r$. We've already calculated that for our coffee data: $r = -.50$ (@tbl-r-definitional).

But like I said, we don't test the $r$ statistic itself. Rather, we need to convert the $r$ value into a kind of $t$ statistic to see how improbable it is, given the variability in the data, that we would have observed an association this strong or stronger if no association actually exists in the population, as our null hypothesis assumes.

So first, recall the general conceptual form of any $t$ statistic (@eq-t-structure). It's composed of a sample statistic minus a population parameter in the numerator and a standard error in the denominator, to reveal how much your observed sample statistic deviates from the null expected value in relation to the standard error---the amount you'd expect the sample to deviate from the population value due to sampling error.

So the specific form that takes here is:

$$ t = \frac{r - \rho}{s_r} $$ {#eq-correlation-t}

Here $r$ is the correlation coefficient, $\rho$ is the population correlation assumed by the null hypothesis (zero), and $s_r$ is the standard error of the correlation. That standard error is found like this:

$$ s_r = \sqrt{\frac{1 - r^2}{n - 2}} $$ {#eq-correlation-se}

For our coffee data, that works out like this:

$$t = \frac{r - \rho}{s_r} = \frac{-.50 - 0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{1 - (-.50)^2}{7 - 2}}} = \frac{-.50}{.387} = -1.29$$

### Step 4: Make a decision

Our $t = -1.29$ falls short of the critical value of $\pm 2.571$ for five degrees of freedom, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis despite the seemingly strong correlation.

::: {#fig-correlation-decision}
{{< interactive-figure correlationTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"t","df":5,"title":"Null distribution: df = 5","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[-5,5],"xTicks":5,"labels":{"x":"t statistic"},"shade":{"tail":"two","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":-2.570582,"label":"−2.571","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":2.570582,"label":"+2.571","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":-1.290994,"label":"t = −1.29","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null t distribution with 5 degrees of freedom. The two rejection regions lie beyond ±2.571; the observed t of −1.29 falls between them." >}}

The observed $t = -1.29$ falls between the critical values of the null $t$ distribution with $df = 5$.
:::

The corresponding two-tailed $p$-value is approximately $.25$, well above our $\alpha$ of $.05$.

### Step 5: Estimate the effect, interval, and power

#### Effect size

You may have noticed we haven't calculated a separate measure of effect size here, as we have done in the past. And that's because Pearson's $r$ correlation coefficient actually is itself a measure of effect size. By itself, $r$ tells us how strong the association is in our sample, but not how much evidence it rests on. That's why we had to convert it to a $t$ statistic for the hypothesis test. Remember that effect size is independent of statistical significance.

Pearson's $r$ is a measure of effect size because it quantifies the degree of association between two variables on a standardized scale ranging from negative one to one. And the correlation itself doesn't get bigger just because the sample does. That's why we can have such a strong correlation in our example dataset and yet fail to reject the null hypothesis.

::: {#quiz-correlation-significance}
{{< include quizzes/17-correlation-significance.qmd >}}
:::

And Pearson's $r$ is closely related to another measure of effect size: $r^2$. You might have noticed that $r^2$ showed up in the calculation for the standard error of the correlation. Squaring the correlation gives us the proportion of the variability in one variable that's shared with the other---much like $\eta^2$ in Chapter 14, which gave us the share of the total variability accounted for by differences between the groups. For our coffee data, $r^2 = (-.50)^2 = .25$, so 25% of the variability in test scores is shared with coffee consumption. So it should be no surprise that $r$, $r^2$, and $t$ are all mathematically related. In fact, even Cohen's $d$ is mathematically related to $r$. I'll leave the actual mathematical relationships for anyone algebraically inclined to ponder over. But for us, the point is that these different statistics are all performing related jobs and share similar conceptual foundations.

As for how to interpret Pearson's $r$ as a measure of effect size, you might remember from Chapter 9 that Cohen offered some rules of thumb for interpreting Cohen's $d$. Well, Cohen was also familiar with Pearson's $r$ and offered some rules of thumb for it as well. Cohen suggested that a correlation of .1 should be considered small, .3 medium, and .5 large. However, like I mentioned before, these are just rules of thumb, and Cohen himself strongly cautioned against over-reliance on them.

There's a great recent paper by @funder2019evaluating that looked at what effect sizes are actually typically seen across a wide range of psychological studies, and they suggested evidence-based alternative benchmarks, shown alongside Cohen's in @tbl-r-benchmarks. By their reckoning, an $r$ of .05 is very small when it comes to explaining any single event, but it can add up to something consequential over time. An $r$ of .2 is a medium effect, of some practical use even in the short run, and .3 is large. And an $r$ of .4 or more, in the context of psychological research, is likely to be an overestimate, the authors argued, that will rarely be found again in a large sample or in a replication.

| $r$ | Cohen | Funder and Ozer |
|:--:|:--|:--|
| .05 | | Very small |
| .10 | Small | Small |
| .20 | | Medium |
| .30 | Medium | Large |
| .40 | | Very large |
| .50 | Large | |

: Rough benchmarks for interpreting $r$ as an effect size. {#tbl-r-benchmarks}

To get a feel for what correlations of these sizes look like, here are four point clouds of 100 points each.

::: {.sfs-figure-row}
{{< interactive-figure benchmarkScatterR10 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.1,"n":100,"seed":31},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = .10: barely distinguishable from a circular cloud." >}}

{{< interactive-figure benchmarkScatterR20 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.2,"n":100,"seed":31},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = .20: a very slight upward tilt." >}}

{{< interactive-figure benchmarkScatterR30 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.3,"n":100,"seed":31},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = .30: a visible but loose upward tilt." >}}

{{< interactive-figure benchmarkScatterR40 makeScatterplot options='{"generate":{"r":0.4,"n":100,"seed":31},"style":"minimal","showEllipse":true,"showR":true,"width":220}' fallback="Point cloud with r = .40: a clearer upward tilt, still with plenty of scatter." >}}
:::

So from this you can see how context-dependent our interpretation of effect size should be. I encourage you to keep a note of this paper or just these descriptions of the different effect sizes on hand so they can help you interpret the findings you read about in research papers. Also, when someone tells you about some experimental effect, ask them what the effect size was. If they can't tell you, you should be a little bit skeptical.

For building an intuitive feel for what correlations of different sizes actually look like, spend some time with [Kristoffer Magnusson's interactive correlation visualization](https://rpsychologist.com/correlation/).

## Reporting and interpreting the results

### Reporting results

As always, we need to report the results of our hypothesis test. Here, that statement will include the value of the correlation coefficient, Pearson's $r$, its degrees of freedom, and the $p$-value for the correlation.

> Drinking more coffee was associated with lower test scores, but the correlation did not reach statistical significance; $r(5) = -.50$, $p = .25$.

### Interpreting the results

<!-- PLAN: what failing to reject means here (as in Chapter 12: not "no relationship"; seven pairs can't tell). -->

Say outright that the seven's r = -.50 is much bigger than the full study's -.15, and that this is what small samples do (their interval ran from -.91 to .41; ties to Funder and Ozer on big correlations shrinking in big samples). So chance is now an unlikely explanation. What does the correlation mean? -->

### Correlation and causation

Now, if you know anything about correlation, it's probably that correlation does not equal causation. So let's make this clear. What this means is that if we just observe a correlation between two variables, we should be extremely careful about concluding that one variable is causing changes in the other.

<!-- DRAFT (the rivals, each applied to coffee and test scores):
- Coffee lowers test scores. Surprising, since caffeine is supposed to keep us alert.
- Test scores cause coffee drinking. Here the coffee came before the test, so time order rules this one out. (A variant survives: students expecting to do badly might drink more.)
- Something else is behind both. Who drinks the most coffee on exam morning? Perhaps the students who haven't been sleeping.
- Chance. This is the one the significance test addresses, and the only one. -->

### Accounting for a third variable

<!-- DRAFT: Suppose the study also recorded each student's average nightly sleep over the week before the exam. That sleep came before the morning's coffee, so the coffee can't have caused it. Here are our seven students again, with their sleep. -->

Here it is for all 300 students. -->

: Correlation matrix for coffee, test score, and sleep across all 300 students in the invented study. {#tbl-coffee-sleep-correlations}

<!-- DRAFT: Students who slept less drank more coffee (-.35) and scored lower (.30). The partial correlation is the correlation between X and Y that's left once Z has been accounted for: in effect, the correlation between coffee and test score among students who slept the same amount. It needs only the three correlations. -->

$$ r_{XY \cdot Z} = \frac{r_{XY} - r_{XZ}\,r_{YZ}}{\sqrt{(1 - r_{XZ}^2)(1 - r_{YZ}^2)}} $$ {#eq-partial-r}

$$ r_{XY \cdot Z} = \frac{-.15 - (-.35)(.30)}{\sqrt{(1 - (-.35)^2)(1 - .30^2)}} = \frac{-.045}{.894} = -.05 $$

- What correlational research is for: things that can't or shouldn't be assigned, and prediction. -->

In any case, the point is that causality is difficult to establish and usually requires experiments in which participants are randomly assigned to conditions. We talked about why that is in Chapter 12. For now, just remember that correlation is not the same thing as causation. That doesn't mean that knowing about correlations that exist in the world is useless. Far from it. It just means we have to know the limitations of the data and the statistical techniques we apply to it.
